title: Doing What Matters — stress companion
description: Make space around a difficult moment and choose one small action that matters.

source.title: Doing What Matters in Times of Stress: An Illustrated Guide
source.author: World Health Organization (2020)
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored stress-reflection companion. The publication overview was reviewed; the full PDF could not be retrieved. This is not the full WHO guide or a validated intervention.
source.exclusions: WHO logo, illustrations, audio and third-party material excluded. WHO does not endorse this adaptation. Noncommercial use and ShareAlike terms apply.

sections.title: Arrive in the present
sections.introduction: Choose a manageable moment. You can skip body-focused attention and use a neutral object instead.

prompts.label: Look around slowly. Which three ordinary details tell you where you are right now?
What steady point of contact or nearby object can you notice without needing to change anything?

sections.title: Loosen a thought’s grip
sections.introduction: Write about a thought as an event in your mind, not an instruction you must obey.

prompts.label: What sentence keeps pulling your attention away from what you want to do?
Rewrite it as something your mind is saying. What options become visible when it is a thought rather than a command?

sections.title: Choose a direction
sections.introduction: A useful action can be small and still leave an uncomfortable feeling present.

prompts.label: In this situation, what quality would you like your actions to express?
What is one action lasting a few minutes that would express that quality?
What kind, believable sentence could accompany you while you try it?

title: YearCompass — look back, look ahead
description: Close a chapter and choose what deserves space in the next one.

source.title: YearCompass
source.author: YearCompass
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored short retrospective and planning companion to YearCompass; not the original booklet. Public community-content licensing guide reviewed.
source.exclusions: No source illustrations, third-party quotations, logos, or assessment scores are included.

sections.title: Look back with evidence
sections.introduction: Choose a year or another clearly bounded chapter. Ordinary moments count.

prompts.label: What dates or events mark the beginning and end of this chapter?
Name three moments you would put in its scrapbook and explain why.
What turned out differently from your expectations, and what did you learn?

sections.title: Carry and release
sections.introduction: You do not have to make every unfinished thing into a new obligation.

prompts.label: Which relationship, practice or discovery is worth carrying forward?
Which commitment or expectation can end here? What loose end actually needs attention?

sections.title: Make room ahead
sections.introduction: Choose a direction and a first experiment, not a perfect future self.

prompts.label: What would you like more room for, and what will take less room to make that possible?
Describe a small experiment for the next month and the evidence you will review.
Write a short note to your future self about what you hope they remember.

title: Heart of Resilience — companion reflection
description: Explore a protective pattern and the choices it leaves available.

source.title: The Heart of Resilience Companion Journal
source.author: Dovetail Learning
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored companion to the named Dovetail resource and its publicly described resilience themes. Resource landing page and OER license reviewed; full downloadable worksheet not inspected. Not a transcription or complete adaptation of the source. The source is recommended reading; these are independent prompts, not reconstructed author exercises.
source.exclusions: No source illustrations, third-party quotations, logos, or assessment scores are included.

sections.title: Notice the pattern
sections.introduction: Use an everyday difficulty rather than your hardest experience.

prompts.label: Describe a moment when you went into a familiar protective reaction.
What was that reaction trying to protect: belonging, safety, competence, or something else?
What did it help with immediately, and what did it make harder afterward?

sections.title: Find a little room
sections.introduction: Respect the need while experimenting with another response.

prompts.label: How could you honor the same need without repeating the whole reaction?
Which person, place or reminder makes that alternative easier?
Write the first sentence or movement of your alternative response.

title: Practical Skills for a More Resilient Family — companion
description: Make one recurring family transition easier together.
audience: Parents and caregivers; optional shared family discussion

source.title: Practical Skills for a More Resilient Family
source.author: Dovetail Learning
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored companion to the named Dovetail resource and its publicly described resilience themes. Resource landing page and OER license reviewed; full downloadable worksheet not inspected. Not a transcription or complete adaptation of the source. sections.title: Map a difficult transition
sections.introduction: Describe behavior without assigning blame or guessing motives.

prompts.label: Choose a transition such as leaving home or settling in. What happens just before it becomes difficult?
What might each person need during that transition? Mark guesses as guesses.
When has this gone a little better, and what was different?

sections.title: Try a shared adjustment
sections.introduction: Invite participation; do not use this page to write rules for someone else.

prompts.label: How will you ask each person what would help?
What small environmental or timing change could you try together?
When will you compare what worked, and how can anyone request a revision?

title: Practical Centering Skills — personal companion
description: Find an accessible pause before a demanding response.

source.title: Practical Centering Skills for Personal Resilience
source.author: Dovetail Learning
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored companion to the named Dovetail resource and its publicly described resilience themes. Resource landing page and OER license reviewed; full downloadable worksheet not inspected. Not a transcription or complete adaptation of the source. The source is recommended reading; these are independent prompts, not reconstructed author exercises.
source.exclusions: No source illustrations, third-party quotations, logos, or assessment scores are included.

sections.title: Recognize your signal
sections.introduction: No special posture or breathing technique is required.

prompts.label: What early sign tells you that you are reacting faster than you want?
Choose a neutral sight, sound or point of contact you can notice comfortably.
Try a brief pause using that anchor. Describe what you noticed without grading it.

sections.title: Return on purpose
sections.introduction: A pause is preparation for a response, not an obligation to feel calm.

prompts.label: What needs a response now, and what can wait?
Write a short phrase you could use to ask for time.
Where could you put a reminder that would be visible before the next demanding moment?

title: We Are Resilient — student companion
description: Think through a school-day challenge and a realistic source of support.
audience: Students in grades 6–12; optional trusted-adult support

source.title: We Are Resilient Student Workbook
source.author: Dovetail Learning
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored companion to the named Dovetail resource and its publicly described resilience themes. Resource landing page and OER license reviewed; full downloadable worksheet not inspected. Not a transcription or complete adaptation of the source. The source is recommended reading; these are independent prompts, not reconstructed author exercises.
source.exclusions: No source illustrations, third-party quotations, logos, or assessment scores are included.

sections.title: One school-day scene
sections.introduction: You can use a made-up example. Do not record someone else’s private information.

prompts.label: Describe a moment at school when joining in, speaking up or asking for help felt difficult.
What did you know for sure, and what were you guessing about what others thought?
What did you do that showed effort, care or courage, even if the outcome was disappointing?

sections.title: Build your next option
sections.introduction: You can stop or skip any prompt. A trusted adult can help with situations that feel unsafe.

prompts.label: Who at school or at home could listen without making the situation worse?
Write the first sentence you could use to ask that person for help.
What is one safe, realistic next step that remains under your control?

title: Empathizing — family companion
description: Practice checking another person’s experience instead of assuming it.
audience: Parents, caregivers and consenting family participants

source.title: Connecting Skill Family Activity – Empathizing
source.author: Dovetail Learning
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored companion to the named Dovetail resource and its publicly described resilience themes. Resource landing page and OER license reviewed; full downloadable worksheet not inspected. Not a transcription or complete adaptation of the source. The source is recommended reading; these are independent prompts, not reconstructed author exercises.
source.exclusions: No source illustrations, third-party quotations, logos, or assessment scores are included.

sections.title: Listen for their meaning
sections.introduction: Choose a low-stakes conversation with someone willing to take part.

prompts.label: What did the other person actually say mattered to them?
What are you inferring about their feelings, and what remains unknown?
Write a question that lets them correct your understanding.

sections.title: Respond without taking over
sections.introduction: Understanding someone does not require agreement or solving everything.

prompts.label: Draft a brief reflection of their experience in your own words.
How could you ask whether they want listening, practical help or space?
After checking, what did you get right and what did you revise?

title: Honoring Agreements — family companion
description: Turn a vague expectation into an agreement people can actually keep.
audience: Parents, caregivers and consenting family participants

source.title: Collaborating Skill Family Activity – Honoring Agreements
source.author: Dovetail Learning
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored companion to the named Dovetail resource and its publicly described resilience themes. Resource landing page and OER license reviewed; full downloadable worksheet not inspected. Not a transcription or complete adaptation of the source. The source is recommended reading; these are independent prompts, not reconstructed author exercises.
source.exclusions: No source illustrations, third-party quotations, logos, or assessment scores are included.

sections.title: Make the agreement explicit
sections.introduction: Choose one small recurring issue. Participation must be voluntary.

prompts.label: Which expectation is currently understood differently by different people?
What does each person say is possible, and what constraints need to be respected?
Draft who will do what, when, and how everyone will know it is done.

sections.title: Plan for real life
sections.introduction: A missed agreement is a reason to communicate and repair, not to invent a punishment.

prompts.label: What is the most likely obstacle, and what reminder or resource could reduce it?
How will someone signal early that they cannot keep the agreement?
What fair repair and review process can everyone accept?

title: Family Well-Being for the Greater Good — parent companion
description: Reflect on caregiver support, connection and contribution.
audience: Parents and caregivers; original source aimed at parenting practitioners

source.title: Family Well-Being for the Greater Good: A science-based workbook for people supporting parents
source.author: Greater Good Science Center (2025); project leads Maryam Abdullah and Megan Bander
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored parent-facing companion on caregiver support and community. Original workbook is for parenting practitioners. Public overview and indexed license notice reviewed; full 27 MB PDF was not inspected. No claim to reproduce its lessons or evidence base.
source.exclusions: No source illustrations, third-party quotations, logos, or assessment scores are included.

sections.title: Include the caregiver
sections.introduction: The source serves parenting practitioners. These original prompts are for a parent or caregiver’s own reflection.

prompts.label: What invisible work are you carrying that someone else may not notice?
Recall a small experience that helped you feel like a person beyond your caregiving role.
What concrete kind of support would make this week more workable?

sections.title: Connect outward
sections.introduction: Choose an action that fits your available time and resources.

prompts.label: Who or what already supports your household: people, groups, places or services?
Draft a specific request that gives someone an easy way to say yes, no or offer an alternative.
What small contribution could you offer freely without adding unsustainable work?

title: Creating a Healthier Life — wellness companion
description: Look across eight life dimensions without turning them into a score.

source.title: Creating a Healthier Life: A Step-by-Step Guide to Wellness
source.author: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (2016)
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored companion to the eight wellness dimensions in the official publication summary; full PDF retrieval was unavailable. New companion text is CC BY 4.0.
source.exclusions: Third-party copyrighted material excluded. Preserve applicable SAMHSA publication notices; this catalog does not authorize fee-based distribution of source publications. No SAMHSA endorsement.

sections.title: Look across your life
sections.introduction: Consider social, environmental, physical, emotional, spiritual, occupational, intellectual and financial life. Spiritual can mean meaning or purpose.

prompts.label: Which two dimensions already support you? Give a concrete example for each.
Which dimension feels constrained, and what outside conditions contribute?
How does that pressure spill into another dimension?

sections.title: Choose a feasible change
sections.introduction: You do not need to improve every dimension at once.

prompts.label: Which small change could help more than one dimension?
What resource, accommodation or practical help would make the change possible?
What will you try, for how long, and what observable difference would make it worth keeping?

title: Anger Management — cues and choices
description: Map an anger episode and prepare a safe pause and repair.

source.title: Anger Management for Substance Use Disorder and Mental Health Clients: Participant Workbook
source.author: Patrick M. Reilly, Michael S. Shopshire, Timothy C. Durazzo and Torri A. Campbell; SAMHSA (2019)
source.adaptation: Aurboda short adaptation of events/cues and timeout planning (sessions 2–3), with original repair prompts. Not the complete 12-session treatment workbook. New companion text is CC BY 4.0.
source.exclusions: Public-domain notice excludes material taken from copyrighted sources. Reproduction or distribution of the publication for a fee requires specific written authorization from SAMHSA Office of Communications. No third-party material, anger-meter scoring, or endorsement included.

sections.title: Separate event, cues and action
sections.introduction: Use a past, manageable event. This short reflection is not the source’s treatment program.

prompts.label: What happened that another observer could have seen or heard?
What early body, behavior, feeling and thought cues preceded your response?
What did you do next, and what effects did that behavior have?

sections.title: Prepare a timeout
sections.introduction: A timeout protects safety; it is not a threat or a way to prevent someone leaving.

prompts.label: What early cue will tell you to pause, and what words will you use?
Where can you take a safe break, and how will you arrange a mutually acceptable time to revisit the issue?
What responsibility can you take afterward, and what respectful request can you make without blaming or intimidation?

title: Thought Records — companion
description: Examine one interpretation against the available evidence.

source.title: Thought Records
source.author: Katherine Clark / Essential Life Skills
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored companion adapting the purpose described in the free worksheet listing; not a transcription of the PDF. Original attribution is retained here. No clinical scoring or daily tracking is imported.
source.exclusions: No source illustrations, third-party quotations, logos, or assessment scores are included.

sections.title: Capture the moment
sections.introduction: Use a specific event, not a verdict about your whole life.

prompts.label: Describe what happened and the thought that immediately followed.
What did that thought imply about you, another person or the future?
What feeling or urge followed, and what did you do?

sections.title: Examine the claim
sections.introduction: An alternative should be credible rather than artificially positive.

prompts.label: What observations support the thought, and what observations complicate it?
Write a more complete interpretation that includes uncertainty.
What small action or question could help distinguish between the interpretations?

title: Work in Progress — companion
description: Make quiet progress visible without demanding a finished self.

source.title: Work in Progress
source.author: Katherine Clark / Essential Life Skills
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored companion adapting the purpose described in the free worksheet listing; not a transcription of the PDF. Original attribution is retained here. No clinical scoring or daily tracking is imported.
source.exclusions: No source illustrations, third-party quotations, logos, or assessment scores are included.

sections.title: Gather evidence of effort
sections.introduction: Look back over a meaningful period rather than rating today.

prompts.label: What have you tried that would have been harder for you in the past?
What preparation, restraint or recovery took effort but was easy to overlook?
Which attempt taught you something even though it did not work?

sections.title: Choose what deserves repetition
sections.introduction: Progress can include changing a strategy or asking for help.

prompts.label: What conditions helped your best attempt happen?
Write a fair description of your contribution without minimizing it or exaggerating it.
Which useful condition or action will you repeat next, and which burden can you stop carrying?

title: Managing Stress — companion
description: Match a practical response to a particular source of pressure.

source.title: Managing Stress
source.author: Katherine Clark / Essential Life Skills
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored companion adapting the purpose described in the free worksheet listing; not a transcription of the PDF. Original attribution is retained here. No clinical scoring or daily tracking is imported.
source.exclusions: No source illustrations, third-party quotations, logos, or assessment scores are included.

sections.title: Name the pressure
sections.introduction: Work on one stressor; you do not need a complete inventory.

prompts.label: What demand is exceeding your available time, energy or resources?
Which part can you change directly, influence with help, or only respond to?
What have you tried, and what happened afterward?

sections.title: Match the response
sections.introduction: Consider changing the demand, seeking support or making recovery easier.

prompts.label: Which response addresses the actual source of pressure rather than only postponing it?
What will you prepare or remove to make that response easier to use?
After trying it, what changed in the situation or your ability to handle it?

title: Personal Wellbeing Plan — companion
description: Write a usable early-support plan in your own language.

source.title: Personal Wellbeing Plan
source.author: Katherine Clark / Essential Life Skills
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored companion adapting the purpose described in the free worksheet listing; not a transcription of the PDF. Original attribution is retained here. No clinical scoring or daily tracking is imported.
source.exclusions: No source illustrations, third-party quotations, logos, or assessment scores are included.

sections.title: Recognize your patterns
sections.introduction: This is a personal support note, not a diagnosis or emergency plan.

prompts.label: When life is manageable, what do your ordinary routines and connections look like?
What changes usually tell you that extra support would help?
Which situations tend to precede those changes?

sections.title: Make help easier to use
sections.introduction: Choose actions that remain possible when your capacity is lower.

prompts.label: What is the smallest helpful action you can take when you notice an early signal?
Who could help, and what specific help would you ask them for?
Where will you keep this plan so you can find it, and when will you update it?

title: Creating Balance — companion
description: Trade one draining demand for something that restores capacity.

source.title: Creating Balance
source.author: Katherine Clark / Essential Life Skills
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored companion adapting the purpose described in the free worksheet listing; not a transcription of the PDF. Original attribution is retained here. No clinical scoring or daily tracking is imported.
source.exclusions: No source illustrations, third-party quotations, logos, or assessment scores are included.

sections.title: Notice the imbalance
sections.introduction: Balance need not mean equal time for everything.

prompts.label: Which type of demand has crowded out other parts of your life recently?
Which activities leave you more able to engage afterward?
What has been absent that you genuinely miss, rather than think you should do?

sections.title: Make a real trade
sections.introduction: Adding restoration without removing anything can create another obligation.

prompts.label: What will you reduce, defer or ask someone else to share?
What modest block of time or space can you protect for what is missing?
What would tell you this trade improved your week, even if the week remained uneven?

title: Understanding Your Own Mental Health — companion
description: Describe personal changes and the support you want others to understand.

source.title: Understanding Your Own Mental Health
source.author: Katherine Clark / Essential Life Skills
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored companion adapting the purpose described in the free worksheet listing; not a transcription of the PDF. Original attribution is retained here. No clinical scoring or daily tracking is imported.
source.exclusions: No source illustrations, third-party quotations, logos, or assessment scores are included.

sections.title: Describe, do not diagnose
sections.introduction: Use your own observations. Patterns can have multiple explanations.

prompts.label: What does being reasonably well look like for you in attention, connection and everyday tasks?
Which changes in those areas would you want to notice earlier?
What contextual factors could explain those changes besides a fixed trait or diagnosis?

sections.title: Translate insight into support
sections.introduction: You decide what to share and with whom.

prompts.label: What have other people done that felt helpful, and what responses made things harder?
Draft a few sentences explaining one change and the support you would prefer.
What unresolved question would you want to discuss with a qualified professional or trusted support person?

title: Emotional First Aid Kit — companion
description: Prepare a small set of accessible comforts and supports.

source.title: Emotional First Aid Kit
source.author: Katherine Clark / Essential Life Skills
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored companion adapting the purpose described in the free worksheet listing; not a transcription of the PDF. Original attribution is retained here. No clinical scoring or daily tracking is imported.
source.exclusions: No source illustrations, third-party quotations, logos, or assessment scores are included.

sections.title: Gather what is useful
sections.introduction: Choose familiar supports that are safe and workable for you.

prompts.label: Which ordinary object, sound or place helps you feel more settled?
What believable words would you want available during a difficult moment?
Who can offer the kind of contact you find useful, and how could you ask?

sections.title: Make the kit reachable
sections.introduction: The kit can be a note, a bag or a small set of shortcuts.

prompts.label: Where will these supports live so you can reach them without searching?
Write a three-step instruction card for a moment when decisions feel difficult.
Which item will you test first, and how will you replace something that does not help?

title: Wall of Resilience — companion
description: Build a picture of the supports beneath your perseverance.

source.title: Wall of Resilience
source.author: Katherine Clark / Essential Life Skills
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored companion adapting the purpose described in the free worksheet listing; not a transcription of the PDF. Original attribution is retained here. No clinical scoring or daily tracking is imported.
source.exclusions: No source illustrations, third-party quotations, logos, or assessment scores are included.

sections.title: Name your building blocks
sections.introduction: Resilience can include help, rest and changed circumstances.

prompts.label: Name a person or community that has supported you, and what they actually did.
Describe a skill you learned through a difficult but manageable experience.
Which practical resource or stable condition has made coping easier?

sections.title: Strengthen the structure
sections.introduction: A wall needs support and maintenance; it does not have to withstand everything alone.

prompts.label: Which support is currently missing or carrying too much weight?
What could strengthen that area through help, practice or an environmental change?
Write a short account of getting through something that credits both your effort and the support around you.

title: Goal Setting — companion
description: Turn one chosen direction into a small, testable commitment.

source.title: Goal Setting Worksheets
source.author: Katherine Clark / Essential Life Skills
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored companion adapting the purpose described in the free worksheet listing; not a transcription of the PDF. Original attribution is retained here. No clinical scoring or daily tracking is imported.
source.exclusions: No source illustrations, third-party quotations, logos, or assessment scores are included.

sections.title: Choose a goal worth the cost
sections.introduction: Choose one goal rather than collecting aspirations.

prompts.label: What concrete outcome do you want, and why is it worth pursuing now?
What time, money or attention will it require, and what are you willing to trade?
What observable evidence would count as enough progress for this first attempt?

sections.title: Make starting easier
sections.introduction: Design for your actual conditions, including interruptions.

prompts.label: What is the first action small enough to do in one sitting?
What obstacle is most likely, and what will you prepare in advance?
Choose a review date. What result would tell you to continue, adjust or stop?

title: Character Laboratory
description: Invent a person whose choices reveal more than their biography.

source.title: Start writing fiction
source.author: Candida Clark / The Open University
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored creative mini-workbook inspired by the course themes of character, setting and genre; a new exercise title, not a separately published OpenLearn workbook.

sections.title: Build your character
sections.introduction: Invent someone rather than profiling a real acquaintance.

prompts.label: Give your character an object they keep despite having no practical use for it. Why do they keep it?
What quality do they proudly claim, and what small behavior contradicts it?
What do they want during the next ten minutes, and what makes it hard to ask?

sections.title: Put them under pressure
sections.introduction: Reveal character through speech, attention and action.

prompts.label: Write a short scene where another person wants the same object or opportunity.
Replace one explanation of personality with a gesture or choice.
Which choice surprised you, and what possibility does it open for a later scene?

title: Places with Personality
description: Build a setting that changes what a character can do.

source.title: Start writing fiction
source.author: Candida Clark / The Open University
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored creative mini-workbook inspired by the course themes of character, setting and genre; a new exercise title, not a separately published OpenLearn workbook.
source.exclusions: All third-party material and images excluded, especially Activity 1 from Fiction Writer’s Workshop by Josip Novakovich (1998). No source literary passage reproduced.

sections.title: Give the place habits
sections.introduction: Use an invented setting or transform an ordinary place you know.

prompts.label: Describe three details that reveal how people use this place, without naming its type.
What unwritten rule would a newcomer discover by making a mistake?
What damaged, repaired or abandoned feature hints at the place’s history?

sections.title: Let the setting act
sections.introduction: The setting can create opportunities and obstacles.

prompts.label: Write a newcomer’s arrival using only details they would notice while seeking something.
Change the lighting, crowd or weather. Which available action changes?
Give the place a one-sentence complaint about its visitors.

title: Genre Switch
description: Tell the same small event through two different genre promises.

source.title: Start writing fiction
source.author: Candida Clark / The Open University
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored creative mini-workbook inspired by the course themes of character, setting and genre; a new exercise title, not a separately published OpenLearn workbook.
source.exclusions: All third-party material and images excluded, especially Activity 1 from Fiction Writer’s Workshop by Josip Novakovich (1998). No source literary passage reproduced.

sections.title: Fix the event
sections.introduction: Keep the basic facts steady so the changes in telling are visible.

prompts.label: Invent an ordinary event involving a delayed delivery, a misplaced key or an unexpected visitor.
List three facts that both versions must preserve.
Choose two genres and describe what readers of each would expect to feel or wonder.

sections.title: Change the promise
sections.introduction: You can write very short versions; a paragraph each is enough.

prompts.label: Write the event in your first genre, choosing details that create its expected effect.
Retell it in the other genre while preserving your three facts.
Which change in pacing, detail or withheld information did the most work?

title: Everyday Treasure Hunt
description: Collect overlooked details and turn one into a story seed.

source.title: Writing what you know
source.author: Derek Neale / The Open University
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored creative mini-workbook inspired by the course themes of observation, senses and memory; a new exercise title, not a separately published OpenLearn workbook.
source.exclusions: All third-party material and images excluded, especially Lesley Glaister’s Memory: the True key to real imagining. No source literary passage reproduced.

sections.title: Search an ordinary patch
sections.introduction: A desk, window or familiar room is enough. Observe without recording strangers’ private information.

prompts.label: List five small details you usually pass over.
Which detail seems out of place? Describe it precisely before explaining it.
Invent three different explanations for that oddity.

sections.title: Choose and transform
sections.introduction: Observation supplies raw material; invention can take it somewhere else.

prompts.label: Pick one detail and describe it using a comparison you have never used before.
Write a short scene in which that detail matters to someone.
What would you look for differently on a second visit to the same patch?

title: Five-Senses Explorer
description: Explore how sensory choices change a description.

source.title: Writing what you know
source.author: Derek Neale / The Open University
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored creative mini-workbook inspired by the course themes of observation, senses and memory; a new exercise title, not a separately published OpenLearn workbook.
source.exclusions: All third-party material and images excluded, especially Lesley Glaister’s Memory: the True key to real imagining. No source literary passage reproduced.

sections.title: Collect impressions
sections.introduction: Use the senses available to you. Never taste unknown objects; imagined or remembered impressions are fine.

prompts.label: Choose a familiar place and collect impressions through sight, sound, touch, smell or taste as available.
Which impression dominates your memory of that place?
What overlooked impression could make the place more specific?

sections.title: Choose a sensory route
sections.introduction: You do not need to include every sense in the finished passage.

prompts.label: Describe the place without relying on visual detail.
Describe it again for someone who has been waiting there for an hour.
Which two details carry the most atmosphere, and which can you remove?

title: Memory Postcards
description: Turn an ordinary memory into a brief, deliberately shaped scene.

source.title: Writing what you know
source.author: Derek Neale / The Open University
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored creative mini-workbook inspired by the course themes of observation, senses and memory; a new exercise title, not a separately published OpenLearn workbook.
source.exclusions: All third-party material and images excluded, especially Lesley Glaister’s Memory: the True key to real imagining. No source literary passage reproduced.

sections.title: Choose a postcard-sized memory
sections.introduction: Choose an easy memory or invent one. You do not need to revisit distressing experiences.

prompts.label: Recall a small moment in a kitchen, journey, garden or other ordinary setting.
Which detail feels vivid, and which parts are uncertain?
Who is the imagined recipient of this postcard, and what would they need explained?

sections.title: Make a small narrative
sections.introduction: Memory and invention can coexist if you mark the distinction for yourself.

prompts.label: Write a short postcard that gives the moment a beginning and an ending.
Rewrite the ending so one earlier detail takes on a different meaning.
Which details came from memory, and which did you invent to shape the scene?

title: Poetry Playground
description: Play with sound, line breaks and surprising comparisons using your own words.

source.title: What is poetry?
source.author: Eva Solzman (as credited in course acknowledgements) / The Open University
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored playful companion exploring poetic choices and invented speakers. Title and prompts are new; not a separately published OpenLearn workbook.
source.exclusions: All third-party poems, excerpts, readings and images listed in the course acknowledgements excluded. Use only your own lines; no imitation of a named living poet is required.

sections.title: Gather language
sections.introduction: No source poem is needed. Ordinary objects are good starting points.

prompts.label: Choose a commonplace object and list five precise words associated with it.
Make a short phrase in which repeated sounds suit or amusingly contradict that object.
Invent a surprising comparison and one concrete detail that makes it work.

sections.title: Try the lines aloud
sections.introduction: There is no required form or correct interpretation.

prompts.label: Write six short lines using your object, phrase and comparison.
Move two line breaks. What becomes emphasized, delayed or ambiguous?
Read it aloud or silently for rhythm. Remove one weak word and choose a title that adds something new.

title: Borrow Another Voice
description: Create an invented speaker with a perspective unlike your own.

source.title: What is poetry?
source.author: Eva Solzman (as credited in course acknowledgements) / The Open University
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored playful companion exploring poetic choices and invented speakers. Title and prompts are new; not a separately published OpenLearn workbook.
source.exclusions: All third-party poems, excerpts, readings and images listed in the course acknowledgements excluded. Use only your own lines; no imitation of a named living poet is required.

sections.title: Invent the speaker
sections.introduction: Borrow a viewpoint, not another author’s lines or a real person’s private experience.

prompts.label: Choose a fictional speaker: an elevator, a patient moon, a retired map or your own invention.
What does this speaker notice that a human observer would miss?
What does the speaker confidently misunderstand?

sections.title: Let the speaker speak
sections.introduction: A distinctive voice comes from attention and attitude as well as vocabulary.

prompts.label: Write a short address from the speaker to someone who never listens.
Let the speaker accidentally reveal a wish they meant to hide.
Which phrase sounds too much like your ordinary voice? Replace it with something this speaker would choose.

title: Pocket Nature Explorer
description: Make a small field note that separates observation from explanation.

source.title: Nature Journaling and Field Notetaking
source.author: Barbra Sobhani, University of Colorado Boulder / SERC
source.adaptation: Aurboda-authored field-observation companion inspired by the named workshop resource; file metadata and reuse terms reviewed, not the full slide deck.
source.exclusions: No source illustrations, third-party quotations, logos, or assessment scores are included.

sections.title: Choose a tiny field site
sections.introduction: A window view, houseplant or accessible outdoor spot works. Observe without disturbing wildlife or collecting unknown plants.

prompts.label: Record the place, approximate time and conditions that might affect what you see.
Describe one small feature in enough detail that you could recognize it again.
Make a sketch in words: note shapes, relative sizes, textures and positions.

sections.title: Ask and revisit
sections.introduction: An unanswered question is a useful outcome.

prompts.label: What question did close observation raise?
Offer two possible explanations and distinguish them from what you directly observed.
What would you compare on a return visit, and what change would surprise you?

title: Writing Adventure Workbook — original companion
description: Take an invented story from a spark to a changed ending; original prompts with recommended reading.

source.title: Writing Exercises Workbook
source.author: Charlie Forêt
source.adaptation: Original Aurboda companion prompts, not copied or adapted from the inaccessible full workbook. The public page states CC BY-NC 4.0; downloading may require free membership. This independently usable companion does not require membership.
source.exclusions: Full workbook not inspected or reproduced. No claim of complete source coverage; no account access or third-party content included.

sections.title: Create the departure
sections.introduction: These are original Aurboda prompts. The recommended Charlie Forêt workbook is separate and was not inspected.

prompts.label: Invent a traveler who is good at something surprisingly unhelpful for their journey.
What must they deliver, recover or decide before sunset?
What comfortable thing must they leave behind to begin?

sections.title: Introduce a detour
sections.introduction: Make the obstacle change the traveler’s options rather than merely delay them.

prompts.label: Write a scene in which a stranger offers a shortcut with an awkward condition.
What choice exposes the traveler’s priorities? Show the choice through action.
How does that choice create a new problem that skill alone cannot solve?

sections.title: Earn a changed ending
sections.introduction: A short ending can leave a larger world outside the frame.

prompts.label: Write an ending in which the mission and the traveler’s original wish no longer mean the same thing.
Bring back an early object or phrase with a changed meaning.
Choose one scene to expand later and leave yourself a concrete starting sentence.
